title: Construct an Isosceles Point
statement: For any segment \(AB\), there is a point \(P\) off line \(AB\) such that \(AP \cong BP\). Therefore triangle \(APB\) is isosceles.
theoremLatex: \text{For every }\overline{AB},\ \text{there is some }P\text{ off line }AB\text{ satisfies }AP \cong BP
summary: Every segment can be the base of an isosceles triangle: construct a point off its line that is equally distant from both endpoints.
proofIdea: Copy the base segment once to create a radius made of two copies of the base. Two circles with that common radius have explicit inside and outside witnesses, so circle-circle continuity gives intersections. Each intersection is the same radius from both endpoints, producing an isosceles triangle.
explorationPrompt: Change the base length and follow the two equal-radius circles. Each intersection remains the same distance from A and B, even though the proof needs continuity to guarantee that those intersections exist.

proofSteps.title: Copy the base segment once
proofSteps.detail: Extend segment AB past B to C and copy AB onto BC, so AB ≅ BC. Segment AC is therefore made of two copies of AB.

proofSteps.title: Draw two circles with that radius
proofSteps.detail: Draw the circle centered at A through C and the circle centered at B with radius AC. Both circles use the same radius, made of two copies of the original base segment.

proofSteps.title: Give continuity an inside and an outside witness
proofSteps.detail: Point C lies on the first circle and is inside the circle centered at B, because BC is one copy of AB while AC is two copies. On the ray from A opposite B, copy AC to D. Then D lies on the first circle and BD is three copies of AB, so D is outside the circle centered at B.

proofSteps.title: Apply circle-circle continuity
proofSteps.detail: The first circle has a point C inside the second circle and a point D outside it. Circle-circle continuity therefore gives two distinct intersection points P and Q.

proofSteps.title: Read an isosceles point from an intersection
proofSteps.detail: For either intersection P, AP and BP are both congruent to the common circle radius AC, so AP ≅ BP. If P lay on line AB, one of the three possible betweenness orders would contradict segment addition for those two equal radius lengths; hence P is off line AB and triangle APB is isosceles.
